title: Validity of Wrist-Worn photoplethysmography devices to measure heart rate: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Zhang Y, Weaver RG, Armstrong B, Burkart S, Zhang S, Beets MW
population: 44 articles, 738 effect sizes, 15 brands of wrist-worn PPG devices vs ECG or chest strap
findings: Mean difference vs criterion HR was -0.40 bpm (95% CI -1.64 to 0.83) during sleep, -0.01 bpm (-0.02 to 0.00) at rest and -0.51 bpm (-1.60 to 0.58) during treadmill activities (walking to running).
Mean difference was larger during resistance training (-7.26 bpm, -10.46 to -4.07) and cycling (-4.55 bpm, -7.24 to -1.87).
For resistance training, the mean difference increased by 3 bpm (2.5 to 3.5) per 10 bpm increase in HR.
Authors conclude wrist-worn HR devices have acceptable validity against a criterion for most common activities.
limitations: Pooled mean bias can hide large individual and per-sample errors (limits of agreement not in the abstract); treadmill evidence is mostly laboratory and not outdoor variable-terrain running; 15 brands pooled.
implications: Average wrist HR during steady treadmill-style running is nearly unbiased (about -0.5 bpm), so it may feed TRIMP, with per-sample sanity filters.
Do not extrapolate the low bias to intervals, hills or strength work; mark non-running activity types as lower HR confidence.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, J Sports Sci, 2020, first author Zhang. Abstract read in Europe PMC; all numbers match. Added the rest CI (-0.02 to 0.00) that was missing.
